transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick round of intros before we dive in. I think we have about an hour, so we want to be pragmatic — pull out the acceptance gates and then agree runbook items.
[00:15] Dana (Brightleaf): Thanks Alex. Dana here, product lead. Marcus from SRE and Priya from ML will jump in on the perf bits. Tom from procurement is on for context.
[00:30] Alex (Redwood AE): Awesome. Priya, you want to kick off with the high level of what Brightleaf's trying to validate?
[00:35] Priya (Brightleaf ML): Sure. The short version: we run a summarization feature in our research product that has both interactive short prompts (~20-100 tokens) and longer multi-paragraph summaries (~600-1,200 tokens). We care about both tail latency for the interactive paths and throughput for bulk async jobs.
[00:55] Priya Rao (Redwood SE): Ok got it. So a mixed workload: low-latency streaming for interactive, plus non-streamed batch for the longer ones. Do you have token distribution or sample scripts?
[01:05] Priya (Brightleaf ML): We have a token distribution CSV and some scripts that drive our internal harness — they're node-based, but they're just HTTP clients that hit our current inference endpoint. We'll share them.
[01:15] Marcus (Brightleaf SRE): For capacity, peak concurrency looks like ~120 concurrent interactive sessions during spikes, sustained average 30-40. Batch jobs run overnight but we'd like to test a daytime window too.
[01:28] Alex (Redwood AE): Thanks. Let's map that to POC success criteria. From our side we usually ask for: functional integration (scripts run through our harness), throughput and latency measurements across sample windows, validation of KV-cache warmup behavior, and a quality smoke test so we don't regress output. Does that align?
[01:43] Dana: Yes, though procurement will want clear SLA gates—specifically p95 latency thresholds for interactive and a throughput/latency curve for batch.
[01:50] Tom (Procurement): Right. Also need to know what data residency & SOC2 controls apply — we'll need the security docs.
[01:57] Alex (Redwood AE): We'll push the security pack — SOC2 report, SSO/SAML guide, and the audit-log mechanics. I'll add that to the artifacts.
[02:04] Priya Rao (Redwood SE): On technical approach: we'll recommend two benchmark passes. First a 'sampling' validation run with smaller synthetic traffic to validate the handshake, streaming compatibility and script adapter. Second, a full 2-hour execution window that ramps to targeted concurrency and records p50/p95/p99, token-level cost, and quality flags. For the interactive path we recommend enabling streaming and measuring first-byte and last-byte timings.
[02:28] Marcus: For warmup, our main fear is cold KV-cache causing huge tail spikes. How does Redwood recommend warming KV cache for a mixed workload?
[02:35] Priya Rao: We typically do a lightweight prefix warmup using representative prompts — the harness supports a warmup-phase where it replays the most common prefixes before the measured window. Important note: depending on model variant & quantization (eg q8_0 vs q4h), warmup patterns differ.
[02:51] Priya (Brightleaf ML): Small question — we use a quantized Llama-variant in prod right now, should we match that exactly?
[02:58] Priya Rao: Ideally yes, we'll test on a compatible quantized variant; if we don't have exact parity we document the delta and run a control test.
[03:07] Alex (Redwood AE): Can you walk us through your sample script structure so we can confirm adapter changes?
[03:12] Priya (Brightleaf ML): Sure, it's a small node script that fetches prompts from our queue, constructs the JSON body, sets stream:true for interactive calls, and uses keepalive connections. It does some client-side retry logic. We can share 2-3 versions: interactive client, batch worker and a mixed-mode shim.
[03:28] Priya Rao: Good. Two adapter notes: 1) streaming harness expects SSE/chunked responses — sometimes clients do websocket based streaming and we translate, 2) keep an eye on connection timeouts — the harness reuses sockets for efficiency.
[03:41] Marcus: For telemetry we need per-token latency breakdown and cost tokens. Does Redwood's harness produce token-level traces?
[03:48] Priya Rao: Yes, the runbook includes an option to emit per-token timing and the KV-cache hit-rate trace. It's optional since it generates large logs, but for debugging p99 it's very useful.
[03:58] Dana: On success criteria: can we sketch numbers live? Our initial ask was p95 < 700ms for interactive and p99 < 2.5s for long responses. For batch, we want > 200 requests/min sustained at 95% success.
[04:14] Alex: Those are reasonable starting points. We'll propose two SLA buckets: interactive (streaming) target and batch (non-streaming) target. For the POC we should treat them as soft gates with 'pass/fail' defined by relative improvement vs current provider as well.
[04:29] Tom: And we'll need a cannibalization metric — if cost per call is >20% worse than current provider, we probably won't move forward.
[04:36] Alex: We'll capture unit economics. The benchmark will report per-token cost estimate using the token counts you provide.
[04:43] Priya (Brightleaf ML): About streaming vs non-streaming — our interactive client expects progressive tokens. If there's a fallback to non-streaming the UX degrades. So we need to make sure streaming pass-through works end-to-end including our client-side parsing.
[04:58] Priya Rao: We'll do an adapter compatibility test in the sampling pass — have your interactive client connected to the harness, stream through, confirm SSE framing and edge cases (partial chunk, reconnects).
[05:10] Marcus: Any infra requirements? We have a VPC with egress rules; will you need us to open special ports?
[05:17] Alex: For hosted POC we typically just need outbound to our endpoint and a short-lived API key. For private deployments we'd discuss more. We'll send the network checklist.
[05:26] Marcus: Ok. We really want to test KV-cache behavior over repeated prefixes. How long should the warmup be?
[05:32] Priya Rao: It depends on your prefix distribution. For the interactive path, a 10–15 minute warmup that replays the top 5k prefixes usually gets stable KV hit-rates. For long-form cases you can do a smaller sample per model chunk. We'll instrument the run to show hit-rate rise over time.
[05:48] Priya (Brightleaf ML): That sounds fine. We'll need to coordinate which hours we can run the 2-hour window — daytime is fine but we prefer a midweek slot.
[05:56] Alex: Let's aim for week of 2026-03-08 and you confirm a 2-hour window. In the meantime Alex will share the harness repo link and runbook.
[06:05] Dana: Security questions — what about audit logs and KMS? We need to ensure no keys are stored by third parties.
[06:12] Alex: Redwood can integrate with customer-managed KMS for private deployments and provide audit logs for hosted. For the POC we can offer limited logging and a redaction policy. I'll attach the SOC2 & KMS note.
[06:22] Tom: Great. Pricing/testing costs? We might want a short credit to run the benchmark.
[06:27] Alex: We'll include a small credit allowance for the benchmark and lay out the pricing per token in the spreadsheet.
[06:33] Priya Rao: Operational checklist for sampling pass: 1) exchange scripts, 2) confirm streaming adapter handshake, 3) run warmup with KV trace, 4) full execution window with ramp and steady state, 5) post-run quality checks (sample outputs compared vs baseline).
[06:48] Marcus: On quality checks — we should make sure we capture a small eval set (10-20 prompts) to compare content drift between current infra and Redwood.
[06:55] Priya Rao: Agreed, include a quality seed set. We'll run LM evals and surface hallucination rate, token-level output length variance, and simple BLEU/ROUGE-ish comparators (not perfect but a signal).
[07:06] Dana: Ok recap?
[07:08] Alex: Recap — Alex sends runbook + scripts + pricing by 2026-03-01; Brightleaf provides token histogram + available windows by 2026-03-02; Redwood runs warmup and posts logs by 2026-03-05; Full benchmark week of 2026-03-08; Security docs attached.
[07:22] Tom: Sounds good.
[07:24] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark window.
[07:27] (end)
